_notice: Independent public sources reviewed Nov 6, 2026. Each finding is attributed and is not a blanket verification of the older seed's disputed origin stories.

findings: STEEZY traces Lite Feet's emergence to Harlem around 2004–2005 and lists foundational movement vocabulary.
A 2015 Vulture account places Mr. YouTube and Chrybaby Cozie together at a Harlem basketball game in 2005; origins were communal rather than attributable to one person.
Smithsonian recounts Al B performing at Harlem's Rucker Park beginning in 1981, long before the documented emergence of LiteFeet.
A claim about a dance's origins does not independently identify a single definitive inventor.

findings: Smithsonian's February 2013 article distinguishes the viral online challenge from Harlem's pre-existing dance tradition.
In a 2014 interview, Chrybaby Cozie criticized the meme's detachment from the original Harlem dance.

findings: VICE/Noisey's 2015 reporting describes early Get Lite music and a renewed wave of production around 2011.
The article identifies the duo Hann as Chris Designs and Lil' Live and describes their sample-, clap- and chant-based production.
Vulture's 2015 movement glossary calls Bad One one of the foundational LiteFeet steps and documents individualized versions.
STEEZY's Mr. YouTube syllabus listed Bad One technique and variations in September 2020. These document usage, not a single established creator.
Two independent explanatory sources document Bad One as part of LiteFeet vocabulary; their descriptions do not resolve its precise origin.
Smithsonian traces references to the Harlem Shake before the 2000s and describes its later appearance in music videos.
Vulture's 2015 feature documents the Harlem Shake's continued appearance in LiteFeet routines.

findings: STEEZY includes Tone Wop among its central LiteFeet moves and offers instruction on timing and variations.
Vulture's 2015 piece identifies Tone Wop foot shuffle as a foundational step; no individual creator is conclusively established by these sources.
STEEZY lists Rev Up as an important move and includes instructional variations.
Vulture characterizes Rev Up as a combination drawing from Tone Wop and Chicken Noodle Soup.
Both STEEZY and Vulture describe Lock In as a finishing move that punctuates a LiteFeet routine.
STEEZY lists multiple Lock In training lessons taught by Mr. YouTube.
STEEZY and Vulture both identify shoe tricks as an established part of LiteFeet performances.
Vulture discusses the Adidas Superstar shell toe in connection with the dance's shoe-trick style.
STEEZY and Vulture document hat-based prop tricks as part of LiteFeet performance vocabulary.
Smithsonian reports that Al B danced at Rucker Park starting around 1981 and discusses attribution of the original Harlem Shake.
The article itself acknowledges the broader history and contested claims; use attributed wording instead of certifying sole invention.

findings: STEEZY's instructor biography identifies Mr. YouTube as a Lite Feet creator, recalling his involvement beginning around 2004.
The biography describes founding the Brotherhood team and shows named Lite Feet lessons dated September 17, 2020.
The Dance Enthusiast interviewed Chrybaby Cozie in July 2014 and announced a Barnard workshop held July 27, 2014.
In the interview, Cozie described beginning instruction around 2010 and emphasized transmitting the style's history.

findings: Vulture's 2015 feature identifies Goofy as W.A.F.F.L.E.'s leader and an important Subway Showtime promoter.
VICE reports W.A.F.F.L.E. as We Are Family For Life Entertainment and discusses original music by crew members.
VICE/Noisey's 2015 reporting identifies Kid The Wiz as Randy Vargas and credits him with introducing more samples and chants to LiteFeet production.
The article places Vargas in a wider network of dancers and producers, not as the sole originator of the sound.
